[h1]An accessible fighting game that's one of a kind, although has a few issues[/h1]

Personally wanted to do a partial rewrite of this review since I seem to have discovered [url=https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=3024835922]the Unbalanced Trinity of online gaming[/url] and despite SoulCalibur VI being one such game in that trinity, I feel like it's still worth getting while it's on sale, if only because it's the only fighting game of its kind.

[h1]Gameplay[/h1]
Unlike most fighting games, SoulCalibur is focused around the usage of weapons as toted by the Steam store page. What this means is that you'll see things like giant swords going up against the likes of katanas, daggers, scythes and all sorts of things that really make fights in the game more interesting. As a result, your attacks will range from horizontal and vertical swings and [spoiler]sometimes[/spoiler] a swift kick between a sword swing's frames. Additionally, the typical attack combo in SoulCalibur is usually pretty short, which in turn allows the game to have a significantly lower skill requirement than most fighters, which I personally find is what makes SoulCalibur a fun experience.

My main complaint is that the community seems to think that it's somehow okay for a base game character to be nerfed to the point where they might as well not be in the game because it allows the developers to sell a DLC character that fulfills a similar archetype. That same community seems to also agree that an overpowered character is somehow acceptable as long as they are female and not DLC, since porn addicts will gravitate towards her, and who has time to work for your wins when your pants are halfway down your legs? I already know what to expect from SC7 as a result of this. In fact, my concerns for SCVII more or less mirror my concerns for Killing Floor 3, actually. Unrelated game, but same insanity from the community.

[h1]Character Creation[/h1]
The main reason why SoulCalibur has developed its fanbase: You can play as yourself. Since the third game, the main attraction of the franchise was the Character Creation system and in the case of VI, there's an entire whole mode where it's all about [i]you[/i] (see below section of the review). In regards to the character creation itself, there's quite a lot that is given to you though fans of IV might notice that there's less character creation parts.

Sure, it's nice to be able to stick patterns onto certain colors and also attach stickers onto your body, though because my prior experience with the franchise stems from SoulCalibur IV on the Xbox 360, i actually think i'd rather have more character parts and have less features than the other way around. However, just looking at the #CreateASoul hashtag on social media shows that you can still do a lot of crazy things with the creation mode. Additionally, SoulCalibur VI marks the first time in the franchise where you will get to use guest character fighting styles such as Geralt and 2B. It is likely that the future season pass characters will follow suit.

[h1]Libra of Soul[/h1]

If you're familiar with SoulCalibur II, then you might remember the Weapon Master mode, which was SCII's story mode, taking the player along various story tidbits with singleplayer botmatches to break up the walls of text. The Libra of Soul mode is something similar along those lines, although the quests provided can now randomly show up in between story missions. Also, you play as yourself so no more "your avatar is represented by the main characters of the game". Instead, Libra of Soul will have you start off with a race and weapon of choice, though you will get one of every fighting style's starting weapon as well as the ability to customize your character after the first mission. Dunno what else to say here tbh.

[h1]Soul Chronicle[/h1]

Another story mode of SoulCalibur VI, although following the tale of the main characters rather than yourself. Taking place after the events of the original Soul Edge on Japanese arcades, SoulCalibur VI is effectively a reboot of the series so as to incorporate characters that were introduced in later games such as Raphael and Talim from SC2, Zasalamel from SC3 and some newcomers in the form of Gruuhh** and Azwel. While some may be fans of it, i feel like it's a significant step down from SCIII's Tales of Souls and honestly, the story mode where you take center stage is a heckton more interesting.

**How the actual fuck do you pronounce ø?

[h1]Graphics[/h1]

I dunno what to say here, since it's 2023 now, and my original review had praised how easy it is to run the game at PS4 quality graphics. If my un-Linuxed Steam Machine can run this at 900p60 on Medium Settings, I'm pretty sure you can run this on a Steam Deck with Windows installed on it on high settings. Not too sure about resolution however.

[h1]Online[/h1]

Maybe it's because I've played too much Killing Floor 2 and Mount&Blade that I think there aren't too many issues with the game's netcode but I can see where people are coming from when they disagree with connection stability. There are peak times on when to play the game and rather than the quality of my connection, I'm more concerned about the game's community sending the kind of message they send to the development team regarding future iterations of the franchise. I genuinely wanna know if there are other fighting games where it's somehow okay to nerf characters to pressure DLC purchases, or for a character to be completely busted because porn addiction is somehow a factor for game balance.

[h1]Conclusion[/h1]

Alcoholism aside, SoulCalibur VI is probably the greatest dressup game that has graced the current generation of systems while also providing a solid fighting game experience for both newcomers and veterans of the franchise. I think these types of games are far better enjoyed if you have some IRL friends, roommates or spouse to play local multiplayer with especially when it comes to custom characters. Until someone decides that they want to profit from the problems that this game has, my final verdict's gonna be "wait for a sale if a competitor doesn't show up"

Soul Calibur 6 is a reboot of the series. I bought it because I had fond memories of Soul Calibur 2-4 in my childhood. I wanted to relive some of that greatness.

The fighting mechanics are there. I don't agree with some of the changes they made to some character's move sets but over time you grow accustomed to the changes and learn to embrace them. The core feature of the game is good, not great, but good.

The soundtrack is filled with grand orchestral tunes, much in line with what has been done in the past. If you liked music from earlier games you'll like whats offered in Soul Calibur 6.

Multiplayer is there. There were some missteps at the start but it has improved since then. Its better than it was but there's still those who grumble about it.

Those are the good parts. There's a lot of bad. I will only talk of the two worst.

The single player game offers a "story" mode. The fighting is fine but the narration and writing is atrociously bad. It sounds as though a random high schooler wrote the story line. It is very cringey and I am allergic to cringe. It bothered me to the point where I could only play story mode in short bursts.

The second major fault is what most other reviews touch upon and that is that the predatory sales practices being instituted by the game. Over half the characters are gated by a DLC paywall. All of the characters are being released individually to maximize profits. Even some of the gear from character creation is being held hostage behind a paywall and much of it is gear that is a copy&paste from previous titles of the series. They are making their customers pay money for old content that should have been included in  the base game from the start. You can enjoy the game but it is going to cost you. 

At the time of writing this, if you want all the current content and you act as frugally as possible it will still cost you $90 for the deluxe version (which includes Season pass 1) and an extra $33.99 for season pass 2. There will be a season pass 3 most likely and possibly a season pass 4. If the price of future installments stays the same you're looking at a $155 - $190 purchase for all the bells and whistles. I cannot support these business practices and shoddy workmanship. This is blatantly ripping off a fanbase for all the money its worth.

I will no longer support Soul Calibur in the future. This is a thumbs down from me.

[b]Pros:[/b]
[list]
    [*]One of the most accessible fighting games. The game includes in-depth tutorials (text-only though) if you want to master the mechanics, but it's very easy to grasp the basics.
    [*]Bigger focus on mind games than execution (almost no moves with complex input and combos are much shorter than your typical fighting game).
    [*]Rather than using the lacklustre teenage character replacements they made for SC5, we have returning characters from SC1 to SC3.
    [*]A lot of singleplayer content: An in-depth story mode (around 10 hours long), a large RPG-like mode (haven't beaten it but I've seen other people say it takes 10+ hours to complete), and an extensive character creation/customizaton system.
    [*]The story mode relies primarily on 2D illustrations with only a small amount of real-time cutscenes, but I think this presentation actually lends itself better for telling longer and more varied stories.
    [*]Very good PC port and the game is surprisingly easy to mod (within a few weeks people found ways to modify sound, music, text, textures, and models).
    [*]Despite relying heavily on reused assets, the graphics hold up very well.[/list]

[b]Cons:[/b]
[list]
    [*]Very small roster compared to previous SC games with numerous fan-favourite characters missing.
    [*]Selection of customization items is smaller than SC5.
    [*]No mouse support whatsoever, which is a shame as it would have been very convenient for the character creator.
    [*]While it's not bad, the music did not impress me nearly as much as previous titles in the franchise.
    [*]I like most of the mechanical changes to the gameplay, but the new "Reversal Edge" mechanic (which is little more than rock-paper-scissors) I could do without.
[/list]

It's a solid fighting game that, on a fundamental gameplay level, meets most of my expectations and only falls just short in some regards.

-Pros-

Optimized pretty well, looks and runs smoothly on my rig (GTX 960 GPU and I5-6600k CPU)

A return-to-form in regards to the gameplay, with a couple of the more overtly game changing mechanics introducued in SC5 removed (GI consuming meter, getting counter hit when stepping, brave edge) in favor of bringing back the speed and general pace of Soul Calibur 2. However, some of SC5's less terrible mechanical additions have been carried over as well, making it the best of both worlds in many ways.

Accessible movement mechanics that encourage mobility at all levels of play, moving around is neither as clunky as SC4 or as risky as SC5, there's a degree of freedom in this game that just wasn't present in the last 3 games and that's great.

Satisfyingly responsive controls across the board, none of the characters I've tried felt like garbage to control, though a few characters seemed to have some relatively overtuned gimmicks, such as Nightmare's critical edge - though nothing in this game is without a counter, at least at low to mid levels of play.

Roster that doesn't suck massive goddamn wang like SC5's. All (read: most) of your favorites from 1-3 are back and better than ever.

Fantastic visuals, great soundtrack, and an impressive array of content by modern fighting games standards.

Relatively good netcode, just make sure to find matches with people who are in your region. The game won't hesitate to pit you up against someone with Venezuela tier wifi.

Very fun to play with friends due to the level of customization the game provides, especially if you're not a ranking whore. But if you've got no friends then you can just watch your created character CPUs (and non-CAS characters) duke it out with eachother instead, which is another welcome feature.

Reversal Edge isn't as awful a mechanic as it could've been, there's a lot more depth to it than I (and plenty others) initially thought, though if you don't like rock, paper, scissor mechanics in your fighting games in any fashion, you're probably gonna get frustrated with how often it's used online. If that's the case, don't worry, they're steppable for the most part and coming up against someone who constantly uses them can make for a very easy win depending on how reactive you are.

-Cons-

Tira is the elephant in the room. She's a DLC character that was made and marketed well before the game was even released and is being sold seperately, both as a standalone character and as a part of the season pass. If you don't want support grimy business practices like that, I recommend you don't buy her, at least not now.

Critical edges could use some normalization. Some character's super moves can allow them to circumvent entire mechanics of the game with the press of a single button, like Nightmare's makes him technically invulnerable, gives his entire hitbox GI properties, and does almost half your HP. Yoshimitsu's can function as a near instantaneous full screen whiff punish that, if you do block, puts you in a crouch recovery animation. Kilik's when soul charge buffed is just... insane, and so on. None of this stuff is game breaking, but it's a little frustrating to get punished so harshly by one button moves.

A few mechanics that I didn't like from SC5 were carried over into this game, like guts (a defense boost that kicks in when you're at low health). While these mechanics have been retuned to fit the pace of SC6, I don't think their inclusion ultimately benefits the game in the long run. It's a bit counter intuitive to slow down a game with mechanics like guts when you're adveritising it as a return to the classic style of SoulCalibur.

Only 10 stages is pretty meh, especially when you realize this is a Bamco game and you're likely gonna be paying for new characters just to gain offline access to any upcoming new stages.

No character specific arcade endings sucks.

Overall, it's a good game that I'd consider a must buy for 3D fighting game enthusiast and diehard SoulCalibur fans alike, but I wouldn't say it's quite on the level of a game like SC2 due to a lack of certain features and the addition of others that cripple the game's fun factor. If you like games like Tekken 7, you're probably gonna enjoy it in spite of that.

Probably the least fun and most expensive Soul Calibur to date. Almost every moveset has been altered significantly to accommodate for some the new mechanics, which frankly remove depth from the combat. Overall it makes fighting much clunkier and less fun.

Character creation is also even more watered down than the previous iteration with multiple, paid, absurd modern DLC packs and very little actual customization or unlockables in game. This aspect of the series peaked during Soul Caliber 3 when it was introduced, sadly and has gotten worse with every iteration.

Single Player modes are generally bad but Multiplayer mode has such terrible netcode it's more or less dead. 
Not to mention having 8 paid DLC's on day 1 release, and all character DLC's being previous series default characters with the exception of the crossover ones. They've basically replaced unlocking characters through secrets and gameplay with a new mechanism called swiping your credit card.

To start, I want to say I do not recommend people buy this game. The game is fun, it's a good game at its core but it's abandoned by the developers, online community no longer exists and to get the full experience you need both season passes. Bandai once again ruined what could have been a good fighting game with a greedy buisness model. 

Now for the actual break down of my review. Full disclosure I played this game on the steam deck so my overall time is not accurate since most hours were done offline. I have completed the games story mode and completed the arcade mode, along with some of the other side content the game has to offer. Now that that's out of the way:

Graphics and Gameplay: The game looks great and feels great playing. It captures the soul calibur games prior very well and the new, rebooted story mode is actually really fun. For single player content I was impressed with what they had to offer especially considering what a let down 4 and 5 were in that area. Despite the combat being fun, it is an unbalance and wonky disaster. Nothing makes sense and because of the way the game handles reverals and combos, the stronger characters always have an advantage over the weaker ones. Playing this game for just fun and relaxing, or playing with friends this is fine. But for fighting fans looking for more competitive and balanced playstyle will be seriously disappointed here. 

Character Roster:

This is where the game let me down the most. The base game roster is small and most characters struggle to keep you engaged in playing them. Fan favorites return and all of the important characters are there, however they do not feel nearly as unique and fun as previous entries. This is due to some new mechanics that were added, hard to really explain but most matches end up dissolving into reverals and rock, paper, scissor moments that give the player who wins a significant advantage. Going back to my earlier comment about balance, this makes slower characters or those who don't hit as hard less likely to win. If you aren't playing competitively and don't care about quality this shouldn't bother you to much, but this becomes an issue later into the story mode as you encounter stronger enemies and you will feel helpless against the AI spamming the same, obnoxious moves. With the DLC characters this isn't as bad (go figure) where the extra characters have better balance to them and have more interesting movesets...but that goes back to my earlier comment on why I don't recommend it. 

Customization:

It's...OK. It's better then previous games and there is alot more here. But there is also a lot less due to certain restrictions on equipment, races, and a small variety of alternate weapons. You can now use guest characters weapons and gear, and have a lot more freedom with how you create your characters outfit even being able to alter weapon colors. However most of the vanilla outfits are bland and boring, and you can't mix up certain outfits due to conflicting pants/cape/helmet etc. This makes it way more limited to how you can actually create your character, but thankfully mods fix this. 

Overall:

I give the game a 5/10. I would suggest if you really want to buy it, get it during a sale where you can get the game plus DLC for, I'd say 20 dollars is a fair price. The single player content is good and it is a fun fighting game. It's just a shame that it was abandoned and left in such a poor state.

[h1]Top 10 Reasons Why SC6 Is Awesome[/h1]

10. Character Creation
If you’ve heard anything about the game, it’s probably the character creator. You get to adjust not just your character’s body, but their outfit from a plethora of different pieces; there’s a separate slot for underwear, inner and outer layer of apparel, gloves and shoulder pieces, socks and boots, doodads to wrap around their waist or collarbones. On top of that, there are three accessory options; these range from flowers, to bunny ears, tails, gun holsters, to tiny porcelain cats or Japanese masks, and you can place them practically anywhere. You can also leave any of these out, so if you want your character to wear just an undershirt, or just a leather jacket, you can do it. Moreover, almost every piece of clothing can have a texture laid over it, which you can color and tweak to your liking, allowing for trillions of combinations. Last but not least, it’s important to mention that you can adjust your character’s height and this is the only part of character creation that affects gameplay; shorter heroes have less reach, but deal more damage. You can use this feature to create some surprisingly hard-hitting brawlers.
[url=imgur.com/a/DUnczMF] Check out these characters designed by my friend and myself! [/url]

9. Gameplay Variety
Aside from the character creator, SOULCALIBUR VI is a really solid game. I’ve had a passing interest in fighting games since I was four, but it wasn’t until recently that my interest in them was revitalized, largely thanks to SC6. Unlike many other fighting games, SC6 has a wide array of strategies that allow even beginners to have a good time, where in a different game, a more experienced player would likely wipe them out in an instant. This isn’t to say SC6 is not a skill expressive game; quite the opposite, there’s a large amount of stuff to learn and apply. Only much of that isn’t tied to characters’ movesets.

8. Reversal Edges & Break Attacks
One of those strategies is Reversal Edge (RE). Every character has a move which puts them in a parry-everything state; you hold a button to deflect attacks, then release for a punish. This way you can always dissuade a more aggressive player from knocking you out in an instant. RE’s however leave you heavily exposed if you mistime them, opening you up for a combo, a throw or a super. You can also punish a more defensive player with Break Attacks—moves engulfed in blue lighting, with long windups that mow through RE but not regular guard. Last but not least there are unblockable attacks, which take a long time to charge up, but absolutely wreck shop if they hit, bypassing everything for massive damage.

7. Character Diversity
In SOULCALIBUR most characters move at different speeds, attack at different distances and employ super moves of varying properties. Some characters, like Hwang, can even trade their starting HP for additional moves and damage. About half the roster has mechanics exclusive to them, like Tira’s split personality, Amy’s rose counter, Haohmaru’s rage and so on. Like in any good fighter, there are many characters which seem impossible to deal with it, until you learn more about them and understand that their power comes with easily exploitable weaknesses. Learning how it all works and how to tip the odds in your favor is fantastic.

6. Music
When I first launched the game, I thought the music was quite generic. Until I realized there was actually a way to pick the music for every stage in the game individually from a much larger list. Including all the expansions, there are over 70 tracks to choose from and I was soon able to replace all the music I didn’t like with what I enjoyed better (Hubris from SC2 is a particular favorite of mine).

5. Accessibility
The aforementioned Reversal Edges are just one of the many features that make SC6 approachable. True, if you’re new to the genre, at first you’ll just mash buttons, but the need to hone your skills will arise quickly. Despite the abundance of information to chew through, I found the learning curve of SC6 very pleasant; there’s an in-built encyclopedia that describes not just the characters’ movesets, but more importantly, how to apply them in combat. It goes through many basic tenets of fighting games, such as spacing, applying pressure, paying attention to your surroundings and so on.
This is further helped by the relative absence of long, egregious combos that keep your character suspended in mid-air for eight seconds. Some characters can still do it, but it’s rare. You never feel like your opponent is having fun at your expense.

4. Supers & Buffs
Every character has a unique super which tests the player’s timing, sense of spacing and ability to calculate damage. Some can be blocked with RE, others can be used as a parry move, some deal little damage but can be applied from afar and others have no reach but cannot be blocked otherwise. Knowing those properties can give you a big edge over others, completely throwing them off and filling you with an intense feeling of smug satisfaction. This variety of abilities allows you to express yourself through gameplay in a way that’s very personal. If you lack the confidence to land a super, you can instead spend your gauge on a temporary buff, which grants you damage through the opponent’s guard and unlocks a slew of powerful moves.

3. Story Mode
Initially I was heavily let down by just how dull the game’s story mode was. And while I’m not particularly predisposed towards shōnen anime, the gameplay on offer would eventually open up and the difficulty ramped up substantially. There are ways alleviate the challenge (consumables, upgrades, side quests, mercenaries) if you feel like you aren’t up to it, allowing you to set your own difficulty dynamically, rather than choosing one from the menu. And you will get your ass kicked if you don’t get good. I guarantee it.

2. Ring Outs
Picture this. Your opponent has you cornered. You took some hits; too many to reasonably make a comeback. You know there’s no way you’re gonna beat them legitimately. So what do you do? How about lure them to the edge of the arena, let them overextend, only for you to simply grab them by the limbs and toss them over the ledge, winning instantly. I’ve done this to people a lot and had this happen to me even more times. (And oh boy, how infuriating it is when it happens to you!) It’s ingenious, rewards creativity, punishes blunt force and is a feature I want to see more often. If you are a weirdo and don’t like that, there’s always a way to turn it off before the fight.

1. Fan Service
There is an endearing silliness to SOULCALIBUR’s fan service. Personally I’ve nothing against scantily clad women (and men) beating each other up with katanas, rapiers or whips and it’s definitely given the series a personality all of its own. On top of this, if your character takes damage under certain conditions, part of their equipment will break; it’s not unusual for two fully geared up characters to end up nearly naked by the end of the match. (This feature can be turned off for each individual character, in case you don’t want their costume ruined). What matters the most is that the fan service never gets in the way of a more compelling, sincere experience, nor crosses the boundaries of good taste. The breast slider and jiggle physics are just a nice bonus.
If your Catholic parents think anime is the work of Satan, then perhaps it’s time to move out of the house and enjoy your life.

This is the first ever Soulcalibur I have played and I'm not even completely sure why I am reviewing this, since I only have a really vague understanding of what makes a fighting game good.

I only actually got and played this game because I got it for 5 bucks on sale. What I understand from the bit I played is that it is a weapon focused fighting game with big emphasis on weapon focused, like the entire lore seems to revolve around magical swords and the late 16th century for some reason. If you really like this story, I'm sorry in advance for saying this, and I'm definitely poking a hornet’s nest here, but I found the story very goofy and I ended up skipping all of it after a while. Like I already said, I'm not that experienced with fighting games, but I did play a few of the Mortal Kombat titles and while the story in Mortal Kombat also has its fair share of “interesting" writing, I found it a lot better than this story.

The fighting itself was really fun though. The difficulty scales well during the campaign, from being very easy in the start, but gradually becoming harder and harder, especially for a casual like me. I did learn some of the combos, which were cool I guess, but I also did a lot of button mashing.

There are also quite a few different characters, though I only got to meet some of them. My favorite is probably Sophitia, for more than one reason.

The character creator is also pretty cool, there is quite a lot of clothing and haircut options to choose from and it honestly surprised me a bit that this game has one, I don’t think I have seen that in a fighting game before or at least not with this many choices.

I have no idea if this is considered a good Soulcalibur or not, but I got this for 5 bucks, which to me is a good deal and I’ll definitely recommend it at that price. This is not a game I'm gonna sink hundreds of hours into, but I did enjoy the bit I played. Again, I don’t play many fighting games and I also don’t play a lot of Japanese titles, so if you play a lot of those, just disregard my opinion about this game I guess.

4 Years later, with a dwindling player base and complete abandonment by the developers, its hard to recommend someone buy this game nowadays. 

On a mechanics level, if you're a big fighting game fan this game is pretty likely to piss you off. Shitboxes and tracking verticals everywhere, the game itself is incredibly random and the yomi level is crazy high because of risk/reward of disrespecting your opponents pressure/oki is. After 1700 hours and time spent on nearly half the cast, the game is not nearly as "balanced" as some people in the community will lead you believe. Some characters possess such overwhelmingly strong buttons that they're clearly better than the rest of the cast.  

The design philosophy is whack AF. Characters who are more neutral focused have terrible frames on hit, while mixup stance characters are slinging safe launchers and safe hori mids all over the place. Some characters deadass will soul charge and ring you out from dead center stage. The best zoner in the game also has the strongest command grabs. The Ninja's movement is terrible but the Pirate moves like he's on meth. 

The netcode is delay-based dogshit, nothing new here.

The core fighting mechanics of the game are solid, but I feel like some of the "challenge" modifiers in single player weren't playtested at all, and the AI can go eat a giant bag of dicks. On the higher difficulties, not using any inputs will just cause the AI to become confused, not really doing anything besides using an occasional random attack which may or may not fit the situation, but by god the second you press a button, it will instantly auto counter whatever input you use. It's like playing against someone with some sort of 99% auto-counter/auto-block hack. Even more, the AI can just teleport. I have recorded it being midair one frame, then crouch blocking the next. In short, the AI flat cheats. It forces the player to adopt a playstyle of "What one attack will cheese this AI best?" So you pretty much have to juggle the entire SP, which is frankly just not fun and boring. Plus, the AI likes to abuse using Critical Edge even when they have absolutely no soul charge (Looking at you final boss in a certain pyramid).

What really kills the game for me is it has some SERIOUS issues registering and executing inputs compared to other, FAR more polished games. Most games seem to have a slight 'buffer,' for lack of a better word, where if you input a punch slightly before you can, you'll still execute the punch. Basically, your timing doesn't have to be frame perfect. Soul Calibur seems to have a massive buffer, so you'll input a command, but say you get hit, well when you land, it'll still execute said command within the context of when you inputted. So lets just say you input a sweep kick, but the enemy hits you and sidesteps. After you recover from the hit, even if you change your inputs to reflect the new direction the enemy is in, you'll still sweepkick the ground where they were literal seconds before. If you button mashed, the buffer seems to save two-three of those commands, so you'll uselessly sweep kick the empty ground facing the wrong direction three times in a row, while you helplessly input a horizontal attack in the other direction. Oh, and the Aerial Control is a straight up lie. It will only work for me in the tutorial. In actual fights, though? Doesn't matter what directions I input, I am only going in the direction I was tossed. If the AI decides to juggle, there's absolutely fuckall I can do about it. A fact which the AI is more than happy to abuse on higher difficulties.

The reversal edge thing is kinda cool on the face of it, but I don't like having a luck mechanic in fighting games, which are supposed to be entirely skill based.

The character creator is pretty awesome, not gonna lie.

3/10, I'm going back to Guilty Gear and Skull Girls

Addendum: To make the game more enjoyable, seriously, fixing the AI and the controls would take the game from 3/10 to 9/10 easy. From a technical standpoint, I don't know how that's achieved, I've only ever modded FPS games, and it seems to be an engine problem, but I can't imagine it would take much. Maybe just give the AI realistic reaction times, and give them the same limitations as the player, IE, can't teleport into a crouch block to cancel a juggle, or moves slightly telegraphed instead of Nightmare being idle on frame, and his sword is hitting me in the face literally the next frame? That would be cool and not make me hate the game.

So, I've owned SC6 since launch, and overall, I've been very happy with the game. I feel that there's something for just about every kind of player that might be interested in the game, as SC6 has a fun and extensive single player experience to compliment the standard VS modes and online play. If you want to play nothing but ranked with a standard character, go for it. If you don't want to touch ranked at all, and just want to customize characters or create you own, and/or just play with your friends locally or online, go for it. if you just wanna play through the story modes, go for it. If you're like me, and want to create characters, play ranked matches, play casual online matches, play the stories, and play with friends, or any combination of those things, then go for it.

I feel that the online population, as of this review, is healthy, and that finding matches generally happens at a fairly good speed. Gameplay online has also generally been a positive experience for me, with horrible lag not being common.

I feel that the character creation is the best that it has ever been in the series, so if you like customizing or creating characters, I think you'll have lots of fun here. Though some new equipment has been added for free since launch, I feel as though the amount of equipment in the base game is a bit light, which I'll touch on further in a bit.

The story modes in SC6 are, in my opinion, pretty satisfying. One weak point is that the game has very few animated cutscenes, but there is still plenty of voiced dialogue, and I do like the artwork featured in these modes.  The Soul Chronicle mode features a main story, and an individual story for, as of this review, every character except for 2B. Some of these stories are more eventful than others, but I personally like that you get to see a canon story for these characters. It makes up a larger story that goes beyond the main story, that all of the characters with a story in this mode get to contribute to in some way.

The other story mode is Libra of Soul, which revolves around a character that you create. In certain ways, it's a bit like the Weapon Master mode from SC2. Most of the dialogue in this mode is not voiced, but there is a lot of it, and if you're interested, this mode adds a lot of lore, and in my opinion, gives the player a nice look into the game's world. You can also change the story a bit, depending on your choices.

As for the gameplay itself, I personally find it very enjoyable, and it might just be my favorite SoulCalibur game overall. In my opinion, all of the characters feel distinct and fun to play. The movesets for certain characters, for example, Seong Mi-na, have been revamped a bit, while still feeling familiar, and I feel as though these characters feel very revitalized and a lot more enjoyable to play. I'm generally pleased with the game's balance as well. I generally enjoy SC6's mechanics, such as the Lethal Hit system. The Reversal Edge system seems to have proven to be a bit controversial, but I don't personally feel that it ruins the game, or makes it unenjoyable to play. I believe the Reversal Edge system is set to be tweaked in the upcoming Season 2, so some issues that players have with it may be addressed soon. Edit: As of Season 2, along with the various other gameplay related additions and tweaks, fully charged Reversal Edges can now be blocked, and it seems the community is pretty happy with this change so far.

The main weakness I feel that the game has is that, in my opinion, the base roster and amount of character creation parts the base game has are a bit weak. I feel that the contents of the first season pass help immensely with this, and it looks like even more characters and creation parts will be available for purchase as part of season 2. However, this means that, in my opinion, the game feels a bit incomplete without the first season pass, so I'd have to recommend getting that to beef up the content a bit. Even then, I feel that there are still a number of types of creation parts and characters that the game feels like its missing something without, so if season 2 addresses this well, I'd probably have to recommend getting that content as well. While I feel that the base roster is much, much better than SC5's, there are a number of notable fan-favorite omissions from the pre-SC5 era. I feel as though the DLC characters that are available as of this review, Tira, 2B, Amy, and Cassandra, really help the roster, and hopefully some more fan-favorites return with Season 2. Edit: Hilde has since been revealed and released, and I am really happy with her return, and enjoying playing as her in SC6. Haohmaru is set to be released next. Its also worth noting that a large number of the creation parts that are available as DLC so far are parts returning from previous games. While it is nice to see these parts return, some players might be a bit frustrated that these parts were not available as part of the base game to start with, and that the DLC parts are not mostly/all new parts.

At the end of the day, despite the shortcomings I just mentioned, I really, really enjoy SoulCalibur VI, I just feel as though the game might not feel totally complete to some players without its DLC. If you're a fan of the series, I think you'll have lots of fun with this game. If you're not, and are just looking for a fighting game to play, or just a new game to play in general, I recommend giving SC6 a try. SoulCalibur is my personal favorite fighting game series. The characters are expressive and full of personality, and I feel as though the gameplay is fun, flashy, and exciting. If you don't think you'd want to play ranked matches, or even play online at all, don't worry. I really think that you'd be able to have fun with this game without playing against people online at all. But if you are interested in playing online, I think you'll be able to have plenty of fun there too.

Posting a review for this game today is like posting a review for a discontinued menu item from chili's that hasn't been served for 3 years, but what the hell. I love this game. I love it with an absolute passion. I haven't stopped playing it since I bought it, you can see my hours.

My favorite thing about it is the character creation mode. This game has one of the best character creation systems I've ever used. The body morphing is spectacular, you can make anything from a skinny stick of a person to an enormous muscle-bound man(or woman) tank, to a literal sumo wrestler. You can make their skin whatever color you like. You can individually color almost everything using one of those RGB map things, you can add textures to costume pieces like scales or a floral pattern or fleur de lis, and add stickers to most surfaces. You can add and reshape and resize various objects anywhere on the character at all, there's a reason this game has been used to recreate basically every fictional character under the sun. I've got every save slot available filled with a character save for two, and there is a LOT of slots. I've made the greek pantheon, I've made wonder woman, Gambit from xmen, nightwing, a TON of original characters. If you like character creation, you owe it to yourself to try this game. 

One good thing I LOVE that they've finally added is the ability to toggle which parts of the outfit are breakable. In Soulcalibur there is a mechanic for breaking armor pieces if you do enough damage to either the top, middle, or bottom of the character. Usually the change is pretty minor, a shoulder pad here, a ripped up robe there. But with custom characters, parts will break off completely and you'd often be left with an abomination as outfit parts that were key to their appearance are just gone. Think, the custom head you've crafted using various parts is now all gone. Or worse, half gone. Thankfully now they've added a toggle for whether either the top, middle, or bottom parts will break, the toggle is individual. So you can still have, say, the character lose their helmet, but not the rest of the outfit, as is often my preference. Complete gamechanger for me, so glad it's in the game now.

Then there's the combat. The thing the game purports to be about. I don't play online much if at all, to be honest I prefer to make unique characters and try them out in offline matches. It's pretty addicting to me. I can really get lost in it, just playing match after match after match. Whenever I need something to occupy my mind I just kind of go into the "zone" and play a bunch. I wish I knew more accurate lingo for fighting game stuff but I'm just not a pro fighting game player. I do pretty much just smash bros and SoulCal, and I'm not into the competitive scene at all, so if you want someone with an in depth look at the combat, I'm afraid you'll have to look somewhere else.

The story mode. It can be a little confusing. it's basically one long timeline full of events happening simultaneously across every playable character, so you kind of have to put together the whole picture yourself, it can definitely be a bit daunting. Then there's the mode where you create a custom character to go in your own story. It's this sort of rpgish game mode, where you unlock equipment and levels and stuff. There's a story with side quests, various locations you can visit like points on a little world map. You meet the main characters of the game in an organic way as you travel. It's a pretty fun time, and being able to make a character of your own is always going to be a plus for me.

The online scene? Dead. Deader than dirt. you can find matches sometimes but not a whole ton, it's not like there's NOBODY but a thriving community it is not. However, as I've stated over the course of this review, that is not where the appeal of the game is for me.

To me the SoulCalibur series has always been a creative outlet. I've been making characters in SoulCal since IV back in the xbox 360. If that's the sort of thing you're looking for, here, have a blast, the creator is right up there for me along with the sims games and Saints Row. (not that one.) If you're looking for a competitive scene I... would look elsewhere personally but I'm not the authority on that.

I love this game, but as it is now it's very dead.

Soul Calibur is a series that holds a lot of meaning for me, so I'm naturally biased for it. I was the kind of person who enjoyed SCV when a lot of fans didn't. Guess I didn't care as much that a lot of the cast was swapped out. IDK. 

SCVI is a reboot of the series. Going back to the core of each character you've come to know and love and reestablishing them as something potentially new, or familiar and revised. Either way, I'm a big fan of how true to form characters like Siegfried are, while others like Hwang got a complete makeover and became something new entirely (in a very good way. Dyde looks like a bloodborne hunter). If you're here to pick up your old main stay, they're here, and they feel as familiar as ever, with some tweaks. The biggest change is the meter, which allows for you to either activate supers, or an install that powers you up, and unlocks new combos. Controls are incredibly newcomer friendly, with a lot of things like reversal edge, soul gauge abilities, and so on being set to singular buttons. I usually play fighting games on stick, but Soul Calibur always felt at home on my controller. 

There's lots of single player content, something that the series had been missing for a while. Not only do you have classic arcade mode, but a single player story for all characters, showing you where they are on the timeline, and a "custom character" story called "Libra of Souls", where you make a custom character and play a unique story. 

Now, the actual story segments are told in a very visual novel style manner. A bit of a bummer, but expected seeing as it's obvious that Bamco didn't have enough faith in SCVI to give it the budget it deserves. I'm sure if they did, we'd expect to see something along the lines of Tekken production values. Alas, that is not the case. This lack of budget clearly hit the rest of the game hard, as anything that isn't a new asset is just ripped from Soul Calibur V, and naturally any jank that had carried over as well. 

I love this game. I really do. I could play it off and on forever. It makes me sad that the franchise is basically dead and buried at this point, as I have no love for Tekken, and therefore no where else to get the same thrill. 

If you love the series, you should play SCVI. Online scene is basically dead and gone, but the single player will keep you busy for a while.

Pros:
-Has guest characters Geralt, YorHa Unit 2 Model B and Haohmaru playable.
-The Create-A-Soul mode has more gender fluid armor pieces and even customizable armors the main characters wear.
-Easier combat mechanics and combos
-Lip movements are fully synchronised between Japanese and country languages (At least, with English)
-Yoshimitsu is no longer a posessed wooden doll
-You can make a custom character your own main character in a preset campaign for Libra of Soul mode and make choices that (probably) impact the end of your campaign.
-The customisation is updating almost every 6 months or so, so there's more voices and clothes to choose from.

Cons:
-Some characters previously playable in Soul Calibur 4 are locked behind a paywall ($5-$6 but still)
-Very little weapon selection, maybe up to 6 or 7 weapons per character, where Soul Calibur 4 had 15-26 choices.
-No Star Wars characters (without the help of mods)
-Armor and weapon stats are only visible in Libra of Souls and besides that, the only stat modifiers outside of LoS is height in the Create-A-Soul mode.
-There are 10 stages (18 with DLC), but often cycles between 7 in Arcade.
-AI difficulty becomes more annoying than challenging (Normal+ makes AI use attacks that use the least amount of frames to reach you as your guard is down. Sometimes, this is all they do. Very Hard adds spam guard impacts that don't even appear until blocked, thus countering Inferno's spammable attacks).
-Loading times for subtle selection changes in Create-A-Soul takes 5-6 seconds. This applies to everything but colors and stickers, which doesn't make sense when certain hairstyles break in battle and don't require 5-6 seconds to switch from perfect to torn/cut. 
-Only 1 creation stage is available and has high quality textures and particles which probably add to the load times.
-Armor/Clothing options will cancel out or underlap some other items or clothing (Socks can't be worn with Setsuka's sandals, Yoshimitsu's arms can't be worn with almost all undergarments but his own, shoulder pieces don't single out with single arm clothing/armor). 
-Only 8 stickers are allowed on a maximum of 48 slots of 12 creation items
-The Lizardman and Malefic races doesn't have gender options, as well as a small amount of armors for the Lizardman race and no hair styles for the Shapeshifter or Colossus races.

Summary: Play this if you like Soul Calibur 4 and 5, making custom characters with limited game mechanics, or anime games in general. Don't play this if you expected more (free) content like Soul Calibur 4 had or if you want to have fun playing against AI. I personally will ride this game out until they stop putting in more content, but for you viewers who want to buy the game, just catch a sale like I did in late April/ early May. Game's not worth the whopping $90 to be giving players frustration and broken devices, so get it on sale for $14.

I bought SC6 on a whim because it was on sale and I wanted a FG to play while waiting for the Avatar fighter. So far this has been my favorite game I’ve played this year. 

THE HIGHS: Easy to learn, hard to master. Coming from 2D fighters there is a decent amount you have to unlearn/adjust to, but if you don’t have that baggage the game is intuitive. Most attacks are simple button presses with directions, and you can avoid hits exactly how you’d expect to in 3D space - ex. you can side stepping the big vertical slash. Also most basic moves are standardized (i.e. 1A is typically a sweep like down heavy kick is typically a sweep in Street Fighter) making it simpler. In terms of the characters themselves there is something for almost everyone here, including cool guests 2B and Geralt. 

Create a Soul is what the game is most known for. I’ve spent hours in this mode creating custom characters, but even besides that the single player experience is good. You have arcade mode and Libra of Souls (custom character story mode) is fun and relaxing even if obviously low budget. I haven’t even touched story mode yet and I have 0 complaints. 

There is a good amount of extras. Concept Aart, soundtracks, character bio’s, etc.

THE MID: Training mode is ok. It has most of the expected features for 2018 but doesn’t compare to modern titles. No frame data or hitboxes here. There are however demonstrations of every attack in the Move List, which also goes over some of the move properties.

Speaking of, the move lists are quite long. Lots of room for player expression or experimentation. It’s daunting at first but again lots of things are standardized. The flip side is these long lists make the game knowledge check heavy. That itself isn’t bad, but…

THE LOWS: Tutorial is not only mediocre, it’s located in Libra of Souls for some reason.

The online experience blows. Low player count, no cross-play, and delay based netcode = good luck finding matches outside of discord/friends. If you’re lucky you’ll be able to find someone with 40x your ranked points in a less than ideal connection after 10mins. Bonus if they are using an obnoxious looking CaS, bc that’s allowed in ranked for some god forsaken reason.

Combine all that with the knowledge check heavy gameplay and being a new player makes PvP brutal. You’re constantly clipped by attacks you’ve never seen, or alternatively you have seen them but can’t properly check bc the connection is underwater and you can’t get consistent experience fighting anyone that isn’t Nightmare or Astaroth. You try to supplement your knowledge online it’s YT videos based on old patches and wikis that have more info that in game but not everything.

Verdict: Buy on sale. Good game but not worth $60 in 2026. CaS and single player are great. Still a buy if you are a serious PvP FG player, but temper your expectations.

What have they done to my boy? 

I'm sure the people with 200+ hours will vehemently disagree with this review, but this just isn't a game that is representative of the series I fell in love with back in the 1990s with the original Soul Edge at the arcades and Soul Blade on the PSX. I absolutely adored that game, and fell in love with the strong focus on ancient eastern sword fighting techniques and moves. Li Long was my main followed by Mitsurugi, and to this day there still isn't a song in the series that's as good as Li Long's theme song. But I digress.

What makes me dislike Soul Calibur VI so much? Because you can't do normal fighting. If you were a fan of the original three games or so, with a strong focus on fast attacks and fluid animated techniques with buttery smooth combos, you won't find it readily here. Granted, there are SOME characters who retain that element, such as Kilik, Talim,.Taki, Seong Mina and a bit of Raphael, but trying to just do normal, neutral, basic techniques is actually a challenge here. Why? Because of the funky controls.

Only Circle provides you with neutral normal combos, everything else does something else. Triangle for some characters provides you with a heavy attack that can also be used for combos in conjunction with Circle, but not for all characters, only certain characters. Square does a grab, and 'X' does a deflect/block. Triangle can also be used as a break. It varies per character. 

The biggest offender of having no neutral normals is Geralt. Imagine my surprise when I tried making a character and wanting to use his sword fighting style and testing it only to find you have NO neutral normals. Who thought this was a good idea for a fighting game? Circle has Geralt perform a rune attack and Triangle makes him roll. So you can only start a combo using a special move. Why? Just why...? 

This makes some characters impossibly difficult to use for no discernible reason. 

Now I'm sure the players with 200+ hours will be quick to say, "Hurr, you just have to use the guard cancel into to the special neutral and then it's easy to start a combo so long as you use an air cancel juggle, durr!" No. That's not how normal people play. 

Plus, the stop-and-go nature of the game since it's so heavily focused on guard breaks, special attacks and that awful soul clash mechanic where everything slows down, just ruins the flow of the game horribly. If the clash was something that only happened at critical moments of the fight and with a full meter, I could forgive it, but it's just a normal attack when you hold down the right bumper, which is something you can end up doing inadvertently when just attempting to deflect attacks. 

For some characters this also means that their very smooth and almost flowery-fighting styles are completely disrupted and made extremely disjointed, such as Ivy, where before she had an almost ballet-style rhythm to her attacks thanks to the sword-whip and how it could be used. But now you have to do a lot of stop-and-go attacks to transition her moves, mostly relying on specials rather than the free-flowing combos you could string together that made Soul Calibur and Soul Calibur II feel so fluent. 

And that's really where things fall apart: the fighting just doesn't feel fluent like the older games. Having to rely so much on special attacks and all those annoying fluttery special moves and super attacks just greatly diminishes from how the game feels and the pace of the fights. 

I used to feel like Soul Blade was a good companion fighting game to Bushido Blade, as it was more arcadey while Bushido Blade was more sim oriented, but both did a fantastic job of respecting the traditional sword-based martial arts and feeling fluid and fun to play without over-indulging in the special attacks and flurries of super moves that games like Street Fighter and Fatal Fury were known for. However, now Soul Calibur VI is more super/special-move oriented than even Street Fighter!

What happened?!

This stood out to me a lot more after recently getting back into Virtua Fighter with Sega's re-release of Virtua Fighter 5 on Steam, and just how good that game feels. It's definitely a difficult title to master but it's easy to get into and hard to master in all the right ways. It's also very heavy on focusing on the technique rather than just super specials and flurries of screen-obscuring special effects. 

It's sad because Soul Blade used to feel like a sword version of Virtua Fighter, even though Namco had published both Soul Blade and Tekken. But where Tekken was more fantastical, Soul Blade felt a lot more grounded, again, very similar to the Virtua Fighter series but with swords/weapons. Heck, maybe if Sega revives Fighting Vipers on Steam it will rekindle what the original Soul Blade/Calibur games used to embody?

Anyway, if you really want a good sword fighting game that feels closer to what the original Soul Blade was, you're better off with Hellish Quart. If you want an exercise in frustration feel free to give this game a try, but the over-reliance on complicated special moves to perform basic attacks for some characters will quickly put off some players. 

Oh, and some of the character's stories cannot be completed unless you buy the DLC characters, which is really unfortunate as I have no desire to buy DLC for a game that I'm just not enjoying that much.

EDIT: Quick update, so I don't want to be too negative here and after completing the Soul Chronicle mode for all the characters, I just wanted to say that Yoshimitsu is one of the worst mechanically designed characters in ALL of fighting games here. He has NO normals, NONE. 75% of his neutrals leave him open for punishes or hurts himself. I'm not even joking. I almost threw the controller at the wall after losing in 10 seconds to Sophitia when I turned away, did some flips, spent around and did a Hari-Kari. Like... what?! 

The thing is, it's one of the EASIEST combos to pull off for Yoshimitsu. What were they thinking? Voldo isn't too far off from this either, but at least half his moves don't take his life or restore his opponent's life (imagine doing a grab and giving your opponent back a fraction of their life? Yes, not only does most of Yoshimitsu's moves take his own life but sometimes his grabs will GIVE his opponents life. Insane. I spent an hour on his story alone because I died so many times... and not because the CPU beat me but because I was beating myself...!!!!

Anyway, one last thing: Namco should make a Soulsborne clone starring Siegfried. He has the most compelling story of any character and a game made in similar fashion to Code: Vein starring Siegfried would be an instant seller if it stayed as story focused as his Soul Chronicles journey. I really enjoyed that and his heroic rise, fall, and redemption arc. That's great stuff, and it's a shame Namco sat on his character and this series for so long without exploring that option. Could you imagine a final stage of storming Ostrheinsburg Castle, fighting nightmare, and then finally challenging Inferno? Could have been real epic.

Oh yeah, and Geralt has the best stage music in the game. That is all.

[h1]SOULCALIBUR VI – A Legendary Blade That Lost Its Edge Too Soon[/h1]
[b]I still remember the hype when SOULCALIBUR VI was announced for PC. I practically threw my wallet at the monitor like, “Take it, Bandai Namco! Just take it!” I pre-ordered it without hesitation. After all, this was the franchise that once gave us Ezio Auditore, Kratos, and even Link as guest fighters over the years. If any series knew how to make an entrance, it was Soulcalibur.
And to be fair, this game absolutely delivered… at first.[/b]

[h1]Gameplay & Visuals – Sharp, Stylish, and Satisfying[/h1]
[b]The combat is everything I wanted. Fast-paced, flashy, demanding, but fair. You win because you made the right read, or because you spammed horizontal attacks like a madman (no shame, we’ve all been there).
Mitsurugi remains my samurai king, smooth, deadly, and perfect for dramatic slow-mo victories.
The animations are gorgeous, swords clash like thunder, armor shatters, capes swirl like they’re auditioning for an anime.
And let’s be real, Character Creation Mode alone is worth half the price. I’ve seen abominations in that mode that would make even the Elder Gods tremble.
For those first few months, I was convinced SOULCALIBUR VI would revive the legacy. Finally, I thought. Bandai Namco is paying attention.[/b]

[h1]The Tragic Fall of a Once-Great Warrior[/h1]
[b]But then… the support just stopped.
No major updates. No real esports push. No consistent balance patches. Bandai Namco quietly walked away like a deadbeat parent.
Meanwhile, Tekken and Mortal Kombat were thriving, stealing the spotlight, running world tours, breathing life into their communities. Soulcalibur? Left to gather dust like a legendary sword on a forgotten altar.
I played for 40+ hours, which sounds like a lot, but honestly, for a fighting game I pre-ordered with high expectations, that’s heartbreakingly low.[/b]

[h1]What Happened to the Competitive Spark?[/h1]
[b]There was a time when Soulcalibur stood toe-to-toe with Tekken, Virtua Fighter, and even Dead or Alive in the competitive scene. It had a unique identity, weapons-based dueling, ring-outs, iconic characters.
Then somewhere along the way… it just gave up competing.
They once brought Ezio from Assassin’s Creed into the arena. They introduced Kratos in one of their titles. They knew how to captivate players with legendary crossovers. But SOULCALIBUR VI never truly leaned into that momentum. No big tournaments, no consistent support, no rallying cry for veterans and newcomers alike.
It could have been legendary. Instead, it became quietly forgotten.[/b]

[h1]Pros:[/h1]
[list]
[*]Fantastic and responsive combat system
[*]Gorgeous visuals and animation
[*]Mitsurugi supremacy
[*]Legendary Character Creation Mode (aka Meme Generator 3000)
[*]Great roster + guest characters like Geralt
[/list]
[h1]Cons:[/h1]
[list]
[*]Post-launch support faded faster than my ranked win streak
[*]Competitive scene left to die without ceremony
[*]Lack of long-term replay hooks or live service content
[*]Bandai Namco gave Tekken all the love and left Soulcalibur in the basement
[/list]
[h1]Verdict[/h1]
[b]SOULCALIBUR VI is like meeting an old friend who shows up in glorious armor, swings his sword with pride… and then disappears without saying goodbye.
It’s a fantastic fighting game that deserved better from its creators. If you want stylish combat, creative freedom, and that classic “Final Battle, Fight!” hype — this game still delivers.
Just be ready to love it… and mourn it at the same time.

[h1]Overall game[/h1]

Fantastic entry of the series, probably with both Season 1 & Season 2, is one of the best titles of its series with one of the best casts. Brings in speed and some of the really cool newer stuff of SCV with a bit of its fun modernity while leaving behind the terrible decision of Guard Impact costing meter, and back to its roots when it comes to this mechanic. Also leaving behind the stiffness of SCIV behind, arguably the worst title in the series in terms of free-flowing gameplay... yet the cast selection was great. The game features a ton of customization, character creator, an RPG mode & the online is great despite being delayed-based netcode.

[h1]Character Creation & Custom Modes[/h1]

Character Creation comes back as expansive as its ever been like SCV, but now there's a whole mode called Libra of Souls that intertwines with the main story and fills in the gaps of the overarching story lines as a soft-reboot sort of sequel in an alternate timeline that spans between SoulCalibur 1 & teethering into SoulCalibur 2, and brings elements of both SoulCalibur 3 & SoulCalibur Legends story plot points & characters that would lead into a different future, yet similar, beyond SoulCalibur 4... if they ever decide to expand and continue supporting the series. 

Libra of Souls is like Chronicles of the Sword for SC3, but not nearly as fun nor as ambitious, but you get to use your own character in a simple RPG mode and witness the world building that SC6 is trying to concoct with this Soft-Reset/Soft-Reboot of the series as the "Conduit" (AKA the name terminology they give to your created character).

[h1]Gameplay[/h1]

Gameplay is fast & fun, lots to work with in customization, music is fantastic, online is delayed-based unfortunately but it's some of the best Bandai Namco has to offer pre-Tekken 8. Definitely better than Tekken 7 by several notches. My one complaint, is Reversal Edge as a mechanic... it's easy to spam and kills the flow of the fight, and becomes repetitive... but it's a marvel to watch at first and casuals will probably love the mechanic... besides that, they got everything else right especially movement and speed more akin to SoulCalibur II's speed while keeping some of the complexity of the modernity that SCV brought in gameplay, while also fixing its one blunder which was putting Guard Impact behind meter, this game solves that issue... Guard Impact is finally back to being a regular mechanic like it should always be.

[h1]No Season 3/Pipe dream/Wishlist[/h1]

Unfortunately we never got a Season 3, probably because of COVID which also hampered and threw a wrench at this game's exposure for tournament IRL play & e-sport events. Also it would have been nice to have yet another 4 characters in the mix for sorely missing characters such as: Aeon Calcos (Lizardman), Rock, Algol, and one more Guest if it followed the patterns of past Season Pass... if not, just Yun-Seong... and as a bonus and free update: Edge Master as the Mimic Character that we never had in SCVI, and a Tournament mode that also worked online, to end the SCVI run beautifully... but that would remain a pipe dream.

I was a big fan of Soul Calibur 2 and 4 in the past, so wanted to try this one as well. Soul Calibur series has its fair share of interesting and unique characters, each using their own unique weapon type and fighting style. And not to mention that the latter instalments also have the character creation mode to make your own characters to use in the game.

Now I don't tend to play online, so this review is based on single-player experience only.

This instalment boasts a wide selection of characters, as before. If you already have your favourites from the previous games, you'll find their fighting style still feels familiar and comfortable to use, but also with some new moves. Generally the flow of the fights is great, as you can string some good combos, move in 8-directions, combo and parry, and also perform special moves. The execution of the special moves can cause a bit of a break in the pacing due to them either going into slow motion or being like a mini-cutscene, though most times I didn't mind it too much.

What I find kind of disappointing is the lack of interesting game modes and challenges. There's only an arcade mode, which is actually a time attack mode renamed. Previous games in the series had a bigger variety of modes. For example, Soul Calibur 2 had arcade, time attack and survival mode, not to mention these same modes could be tackled with each character's unique weapons with different bonuses and drawbacks, which often drastically changed the gameplay. Or like Soul Calibur 4 with its brutal Tower of Lost Souls that put us against creative challenges.

There are two separate campaign modes here though. One of them allows us to play the core background story of each character. The other has us create a new character with creation tools and undertake an adventure. But I personally found both of those to be uninteresting. There's a lot of narration and dialogue going on with text and still character portraits before you get to the battles. Usually when I want that, I play visual novels, which have much more interesting storylines. In a fighting game, you want to get into the action quickly, without long breaks of story info dump in between. I think actual cutscenes might've served the story modes better here, but even they would've needed to be short and to the point.

The visuals are generally great. Nice selection of outfits for characters and character creation (there's plenty of eye candy for anyone), and beautiful environments. Music and voice acting are both decent too. I would've liked to feel more impact and oomph from strikes though, particularly with better-chosen sound effects, but what's there is ok. 

Overall, as far as core fighting mechanics go and presentation, Soul Calibur 6 is great, but I personally think it needed more game modes and challenges. Again, I didn't play online, but I can't imagine that many people are playing this game nowadays as it's several years old now. So for this reason I recommend it only when it goes on a big discount.

The shortest description would be "Fun but clearly incomplete, not worth full price."  I like the game but I can't recommend it since it feels like you'd need all the announced DLC (3 chars + 2 armor packs) just to get the character creation options and roster to a reasonable level. 

Some things to note if you're one of those people who'll buy it despite the poor value proposition (like me)

- Inputs have been restructured to reduce the use of G+B and B+K
- ←+G+A replaces G+B for alternate throws
        - ← + any attack breaks these throws, while any attack without a direction breaks normal throws
- Guard Impacts are stronger and easier to use
        - No meter used, all high, mid, low & throws reflected except for guard breaks and unblockables
- A new "Reversal Edge" system has been introduced and can be triggered with G+B or durreing certain combos
        - you enter a brief auto parry stance (can be broken or side stpped easily) followed by a weak attack that can trigger a Rock Paper Scissors type stand off if it hits or is blocked.
- The game still has a meter system but it's been changed
        - The "Brave Edge" system has been removed, but you can still use meter on a super attack like SC5 (A+B+K), or use meter to trigger a "Soul Charge" (←+A+B+K) unlocking upgraded version of your regular move set and giving your attacks chip damage if the opponent blocks them. Soul Charge is a greate replacement for Brave Edges imo

- There are 2 single player modes
        - "MISSION: Libra of Soul" is a throwback to previous games, you make a custom character, level up, buy better weapons, and fight with various restrictions and combat conditions. It's a nice idea but is very dialogue heavy compared to the SCII & III modes it's inspired by, a greater focus on combat variety and conditions would have gone a long way. The main curency in this mode is seprate from Soul Points, which is used to buy creation parts, you can exchange them but don't, the rate is terrible making this mode worthless if you're trying to buy creation parts.
        - Another important note about this mode is that there's a dojo early on that will give you some combat basics. I'd recommend you do some of it, and come back once you've played a bit more to really get a handel on the new mechanics in context.
        - "STORY: Soul Chronicle" is an actual story mode, it features short 25-ish min routs for each character, and a main storyline about the size of 3 normal routs. It's actually pretty well done, the stories themselves are a little short but it's nice getting a fully voiced backstory to all the main characters, one of the strong points of SC6 imo.

- Character creation is limited in strange ways and feels incomplete
        - Unlocking a new creation part required 550 Soul Points, you get 350 from completing a rout in STORY mode, 2000 from completeing the main story rout, and 50 from playing a ranked match, win or lose.
        - Main characters only feature 1 costume with alternate costumes being replaced by  alternate colors, they're fully customizable though
        - The biggest problem is the lack of creation parts, even with the main character parts being available to other main characters and custom characters it's a small selection. This is made worse by the complete lack of new creation parts, I counted just under 30 new parts (including made/female doubles) when you exclude main character parts. The returning parts aren't even in complete sets (e.g. Jesters Hat but nothing else, Gorgon Helmet but nothing else), and the armor selection in general is also very weak.
        - It's restrictive in ways SCV wasn't due to some parts being tied to certain races (a new feature), e.g. elf ears / demon tails are unique to the "Hidden Village Clan" and "Lost Oul" races, but you can't edit them like a regular accessory so you have to accept them as is, along with whatever else the race comes with. Another example of a strange restrictions is the picture frame options, certain frames are now limited to front or back frame only, unlick SC5 where they could be used wherever.
        - The game doesn't feature any kind of mouse support, and it's most annoying in this mode when you're slowely moving sliders or navigating color maps
        - The skin tones are allot higher contracts than I remember from previous games which is an interesting change. But stickers won't exactly match skin tones like they did in SC5, meaning you can't hid parts of stickers like you used to be able to
        - Stickers can be trickey to place since "Place by view" for has been replaced by "Projection" and now also uses sliders. In general the slider use would be allot easier if the visual aids that appear when picking the placement mode could be toggled, it's hard to properly place the stickers when you have time keep in mind the X, Y and projection angle without any visual representation.
        - The sticker and pattern selection is also taken from SC5 with no worthwhile additions, I counted 2 new stickers (maybe) and a new "dirt" category, the same goes for the picture backgrounds, althought they did add 10 new stage backgrounds.
        - They did add allot of options to this mode, but they are mostly to the view screen (pause durring creation, first option), which is useful because you can change the lighting and checking that your color scheme works with all of them. You also have allot more pose options for picture taking, and can set the character's expression, and movemement speed to get the perfect shot. This was actually a really well thought out change, which makes me think if given enough time the rest of the creation mode could have been as well thoughout.

- Since this is the first game to launch with a PC version, mods are a possiblity this time which is probably the best thing to come from SC6 imo, there aren't many but Nexusmods has a small handful (including unlocking an incomplete Lizardman and of course nude mods), I've also seen a bunch of weapon / equipment replacement mods posted to deviantart if you can believe it. You can of course also change the keys to PS4 buttons via mods.
- The menus feel lifeless, it's a minor grip but the lack of an announcer saying "Welcome back to the stage of history" etc. when you load up the game and the generally bland look of the menus really bugs me.

Honestly I really like this version of Soul Calibur, and I think it has allot potential to be great, but it's so clear that just like last time the devs didn't get the time to do as much as they wanted. Althought unlike last time, it feels like they cut corners at the start (no alternate costumes, small roster, limited creation options) to try and fill out the single player modes which were a complete mess in SC5. If the games does well and gets 2 rounds of DLCs and some patches to fix some stupid issues (mouse support, some graphical bugs, remove some creation restrictions) I can see it being truely great. But even then you will still need to shell out for all the DLC + the base game making it hard to recommend, but at least something that I actually can recommend.

Look, there's a lot of downsides. The net-code is delay-based. The single-player content is kinda meh. The player-base is low. Like most fighting games, there's a steep learning curve. There's a lot of veteran players who will obliterate you. But it's the best designed fighting game I've ever played. Learning characters is addictive. The characters are surprisingly balanced. It's so fun to watch competitively.

Let’s get the huge negative out of the way. Custom characters in ranked was a huge mistake. I bought this game on release and it turned me off the game eventually. Custom characters ruin the competitive integrity and spirit of ranked; characters having different heights and hit/hurtboxes from the character that’s being mimicked introduces a wide spectrum of variance in the match. I know SoulCalibur has always had a stronger customization mode and I do agree that it should be celebrated. However, competitive integrity and the customization can and should exist as two separate entities.

Despite that negative, offline tournaments/sessions will always be the gold standard and the game holds up well there.

The new mechanic, Reversal Edge, was somewhat contentious. When a Reversal Edge hits, an RPS minigame occurs, which slows down the match. However, Reversal Edges have an obvious flaw – being very vertical. As skill level increased, the mechanic became used less and less. Consequently, I wasn’t entirely put off by the mechanic’s consequence of slowing the game down since it happened less often over time. Whenever it did happen however, it became more a knowledge check than anything. As an example - like how in Tekken how you’d want to break King’s Rolling Death Cradle if he happened to get the Arm Breaker grab on you…for Reversal Edge, you’ll wanna make sure to defend against Geralt’s A option at all costs, especially for ring out scenarios. Getting hit with non-A options would just be a small price to pay compared to the bigger punishment (unless it’s a low HP situation, then have fun lol).

Therefore, I wouldn’t call Reversal Edge a success, but I don’t think it’s the colossal disaster that some interpret it to be. If they want to do something like this again for the next entry, I would ask Namco to take inspiration from Tekken’s Power Crush or SF4’s Focus Attack. As it is right now, Reversal Edge is awkward and it didn’t exactly help beginners defend better either.

I’ve been fairly critical so far – so why do I still recommend it? I recognize that not all buyers of a fighting game are necessarily tournament players. I enjoyed the package as a whole. The single player content is good and the roster is great too. Geralt, 2B and Haohmaru being available as guest characters still kinda blows my mind. If you’ve played SoulCalibur in the past, the overall presentation and action should scratch that itch. Libra of Souls, Story Mode and of course, Character Creation/Customization should keep most players occupied enough.
